---
title: "How it works"
---

## One process per document

Quarto's engine API hands an engine the whole document and takes markdown
back. So the engine collects every ` ```{er2} ` cell and every inline
expression, in document order, into one JSON job, and starts one process:

```text
er2.js ──JSON job──► python er2_runner.py ──JSON result──► er2.js
                          │
                  er2.preparse, er2.prelude
                          │
                SymPy        cypari2 → PARI
```

`er2_runner.py` ships inside the extension. It runs under the Python ER2
is installed in, executes every cell in one ER2 namespace — which is what
makes state carry across cells — and returns, for each cell, a
notebook-shaped list of outputs: streams, display values with their
LaTeX, figures, and an error if there was one.

Because the result is structured, nothing has to be parsed out of text.
The runner keeps its own copy of the standard output for the result and
captures each cell's output separately — at the Python level, so `print`
and `show` keep their order, and at the file-descriptor level, so C code
such as PARI cannot write into the result.

## Why not Jupyter

ER2 runs in Quarto through its Jupyter kernel too, with ` ```{python} `
cells. But Quarto chooses the engine from a block's language before any
kernel is consulted, and its Jupyter engine does not claim `er2`; so an
` ```{er2} ` block under Jupyter is silently not executed. ER2 measured
this, and decided against an engine that would reimplement Quarto's
Jupyter engine to run a kernel.

This engine is not that engine. It runs ER2 the way PARI-GP-ENGINE runs
gp: as an external program, in batch.

| | `jupyter: er2` | `engine: er2` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cells are written | ` ```{python} ` | ` ```{er2} ` |
| Needs Jupyter | yes | no |
| Kernel daemon | yes | no |
| Editor Python tooling in cells | yes | no |
| Mix with other Python cells | yes | no — one engine per document |

## Highlighting

`er2.xml` is ER2's own syntax definition: `sym`, the `5r` raw literals and
`^^`, then all of Python's rules. The engine hands it to pandoc with a
path relative to the document, so a frozen result replays on any machine.

```er2
sym x, y            # sym in a comment is just a comment
z = x^2 ^^ 3r       # "and ^^ in a string is text"
```
